text.title: Success Metrics Definition Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules every Success Metrics Definition application must enforce, plus a skip-this-methodology fallback. These are HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: Spec MUST cite exactly ONE north-star metric linked to a business outcome.
rule.rationale: Multi-north-stars dilute focus and create conflicting incentives.

rule.statement: Supporting KPIs MUST be ≤5, partitioned across AARRR (max 1 per stage), and MUST collectively cover at least 3 of the 5 AARRR stages. Single-stage KPI sets are rejected.
rule.rationale: More than 5 KPIs nobody reads; AARRR partition ensures funnel coverage. Single-stage coverage hides the funnel — a retention-only KPI set ignores the leak in activation.

rule.statement: Every metric MUST be tagged vanity (look-good, not decision-driving) | actionable (decision-driving). Vanity metrics (pageviews, raw signups without activation) MUST be explicitly listed as excluded and flagged wherever they still appear on a dashboard.
rule.rationale: Vanity exclusions document the discipline; un-flagged vanity re-creeps. Vanity metrics quietly drive feature choices, so explicit per-metric tagging exposes the influence instead of leaving it to the exclusion list alone.

rule.statement: Every KPI MUST carry baseline + target + measurement window, and the target MUST carry a deadline. Targetless metrics are rejected.
rule.rationale: Targets without baselines are wishes; targets without windows are unbounded. A metric without a target and a date is a thermometer, not a decision tool.

rule.statement: Every KPI MUST have an instrumentation status; un-instrumented KPIs park-listed.
rule.rationale: Un-instrumented KPIs become guesswork that erodes trust in the dashboard.

rule.statement: Every metric MUST carry an exact measurement definition: event name, filter rules, time window, exclusions. "Active users" without a definition is rejected.
rule.rationale: Without exact definitions teams argue about numbers; with definitions they argue about strategy. An undefined DAU leaves nobody able to say whether admin and test accounts are inside it.

rule.statement: The spec MUST name a single accountable owner (a person, not "the team"), and the north-star MUST name its owner separately.
rule.rationale: Metric sets without a named owner become folklore inside two quarters; the output contract already carries an `owner` field, and the rule is what makes it non-optional.

rule.statement: If any Applies-If precondition fails OR any Skip-If condition triggers, do NOT apply this methodology. Emit a skip-record naming the failed precondition / triggered skip, and route the task to the correct methodology (or none).
rule.rationale: Mis-application produces worse artefacts than no methodology, because downstream consumers trust the schema; the skip-record makes non-application traceable.
